distinguishing_text: Because patients with neurogenic bladder have a real, chronically elevated baseline risk of urinary tract infection (from impaired emptying, catheter use, and altered bladder defence mechanisms), an acute UTI can present as an acute worsening of otherwise-stable storage or voiding symptoms, new incontinence, or in SCI patients even as autonomic dysreflexia or non-specific systemic illness rather than classic dysuria (due to impaired bladder sensation). The distinguishing feature is a positive urine culture (a bacterial concentration of >=10^3 CFU/mL together with symptoms is the accepted diagn

distinguishing_text: Fowler's syndrome is a real, distinct cause of chronic urinary retention in young women, characterised by impaired urethral sphincter relaxation (abnormal sphincter EMG activity) without a demonstrable central or peripheral neurological lesion on standard workup, often associated with polycystic ovary syndrome. It is listed among the neurogenic-mimicking causes of detrusor underactivity/retention specifically because it must be distinguished from true neurogenic (SCI/MS/diabetic) retention through the absence of an identifiable causative neurological disease and characteristic sphincter EMG fi

Sigmoid and cecal volvulus are real, mechanistically distinct differentials/causes of LBO (accounting for a real 3-8% and 1-3% of LBO cases respectively, per Radiopaedia), and small-bowel volvulus is a real, rarer cause of SBO. This knowledge base's own separate 'volvulus' entry covers that condition's specific twisting mechanism, imaging signs (coffee bean, bird's beak, whirl and corkscrew signs), and outcome data in full, and is cross-referenced here rather than duplicated.

Real physiological uretero-hydronephrosis of pregnancy is right-sided-predominant (63% in a 100-patient MRI cohort), typically confined to the kidney and/or proximal ureter, asymptomatic, and does not require intervention; left-sided or whole-ureter dilation in a pregnant patient is real evidence favoring a pathological cause (stone, true obstruction) rather than physiological dilation, per the same MRI study's own practical conclusion.

Migraine without aura (ICHD-3 1.1) requires at least 2 of 4 different pain characteristics -- unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate-severe intensity, aggravation by routine physical activity -- plus nausea/vomiting and/or both photophobia AND phonophobia, and attacks last 4-72 hours untreated; this contrasts point-for-point with TTH's bilateral, pressing, mild-moderate, activity-tolerant pattern with at most one of photophobia/phonophobia and no vomiting. See this knowledge base's own 'migraine' entry for full ICHD-3 migraine criteria detail. In practice the two disorders frequently

Migraine differs from cluster headache in: longer attack duration (4-72 hours vs 15-180 minutes); more often bilateral pain, pulsating quality; patients seeking stillness/quiet dark rooms rather than restlessness; associated nausea/vomiting and photophobia+phonophobia (rather than ipsilateral cranial autonomic signs) as the defining associated features; and a female predominance (roughly 3:1) in contrast to cluster headache's strong male predominance.

Classical trigeminal neuralgia (ICHD-3 13.1.1) causes paroxysms of unilateral facial pain confined to one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (most often V2/V3, sparing the periorbital autonomic pattern of cluster headache), described as electric-shock-like, shooting, stabbing or sharp, lasting from a fraction of a second up to two minutes, and classically precipitated by innocuous stimuli in the trigger zone (light touch, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, cold wind) - a precipitation pattern not seen in cluster headache. It lacks the prominent ipsilateral autonomic features and restless

The single most important bedside discriminator is FOREHEAD SPARING: because the upper face (frontalis, orbicularis oculi) receives bilateral cortical corticobulbar innervation while the lower face receives only contralateral innervation, a central lesion (stroke) spares the forehead - the patient can still wrinkle the forehead and close the eye on the affected side, with weakness confined to the lower face. Preserved forehead strength should immediately raise suspicion for a central cause rather than Bell's palsy. Any equivocal presentation must be triaged as a possible stroke (see EMERGENCY_

Caused by VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, Ramsay Hunt presents with the classic triad of peripheral facial nerve palsy, ear pain, and a vesicular zoster rash in the ear canal/pinna (vesicles can also appear in the mouth); it can also cause sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo. HSV-1 PCR of facial nerve fluid is negative in Ramsay Hunt (versus 79% positive in true Bell's palsy), and prognosis for full recovery is generally worse than Bell's palsy, so it changes both prognosis-counseling and the choice/urgency of antiviral therapy.

Lyme disease should be specifically considered with BILATERAL facial palsy (which is rare overall, 0.3%-2.0% of all facial palsy presentations, and 'red-flag' for a systemic cause rather than idiopathic Bell's), or with a history of tick exposure, travel/residence in a Lyme-endemic area, or an antecedent erythema migrans rash; Lyme disease is reported as the most common infectious cause of bilateral facial nerve palsy in the pediatric population. Diagnosis requires Lyme serology, and treatment is antibiotic-based rather than the standard Bell's palsy steroid/antiviral approach.

confusable_name_raw: Tumor / structural lesion (facial nerve schwannoma, parotid gland tumor, cerebellopontine-angle mass, leptomeningeal metastasis)
distinguishing_text: Suspect a structural lesion rather than idiopathic Bell's palsy when the palsy is slowly/insidiously progressive rather than acute, when there are other cranial neuropathies or a palpable parotid mass, or - as shown in a recent structural-mimic case series - when facial palsy RECURS strictly on the same (ipsilateral) side with progressively worsening House-Brackmann grade and progressive axonal loss on serial nerve conduction studies across episodes; such a pattern should prompt dedicated facial-nerve MRI rather than repeated 'recurrent Bell's palsy' labeling.

Alzheimer's disease classically presents with an insidious, gradually and steadily progressive amnestic syndrome (impaired new learning/episodic memory as the earliest and most prominent feature) without a stepwise course, focal neurological signs, or early gait/urinary symptoms; medial temporal (hippocampal/entorhinal) atrophy is disproportionate to any vascular lesion load on imaging. Vascular dementia instead shows (in its classic form) a stepwise or fluctuating course tied to vascular events, executive-predominant over memory-predominant impairment, focal neurological signs, and imaging-co

Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) can mimic the executive-dysfunction/personality-change picture of vascular dementia, but the revised international consensus criteria require early, progressive change in personality/behaviour (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseverative/compulsive behaviour, hyperorality) with relatively preserved episodic memory and visuospatial skills, typically without focal vascular signs, and with frontal/anterior temporal atrophy or hypometabolism on imaging rather than infarcts or a vascular lesion pattern. Gliomas are intra-axial (arising from brain parenchyma) versus meningioma's extra-axial dural-based location; gliomas typically lack a dural tail sign and show infiltrative rather than well-circumscribed margins. This knowledge base does not currently contain a separate 'glioma' entry to cross-reference directly - noted here rather than fabricating a cross-link.

confusable_name_raw: Bacterial or viral (aseptic) meningitis without brain parenchymal involvement
distinguishing_text: Meningitis produces fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia but, unlike encephalitis, does not typically cause altered mental status persisting >=24h, seizures, or focal neurological deficits; when these are present the case should be classified and worked up as encephalitis (or meningoencephalitis) rather than uncomplicated meningitis, per the consensus case-definition framework.

confusable_name_raw: Anti-NMDA-receptor (and other autoimmune) encephalitis presenting as a primary psychiatric disorder
distinguishing_text: Because psychiatric symptoms or memory problems are the presenting feature in essentially all anti-NMDAR cases, patients (especially young women) are frequently first evaluated or admitted for a presumed primary psychiatric illness (e.g. new-onset psychosis, catatonia) before seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability or decreased consciousness emerge and prompt neurological/CSF antibody work-up; this misdiagnosis risk is explicitly highlighted in the foundational case series.

ADEM is a monophasic, typically post-infectious or post-vaccination inflammatory demyelinating disease of the CNS, generally affecting children, with multifocal white-matter lesions on MRI rather than the focal medial-temporal pattern of HSV encephalitis or the normal/non-specific MRI often seen in anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it sits within the same broad differential as infectious/autoimmune encephalitis and formal revised case definitions for ADEM versus other CNS demyelinating/inflammatory syndromes have been published.

Distinguishing iNPH from Alzheimer's disease matters because the two commonly coexist in the same elderly patient (mixed pathology is frequent) and because iNPH cognitive impairment is a frontal-subcortical/dysexecutive pattern with relative sparing of episodic memory encoding and cortical functions early on, versus the primarily amnestic, hippocampal-medial-temporal pattern of early Alzheimer's disease; gait is classically normal early in pure Alzheimer's disease but is required for an iNPH diagnosis from the outset. Panic disorder and agoraphobia are now diagnosed as separate, potentially co-occurring conditions rather than one being a subtype of the other. Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus persistent concern/worry about additional attacks or their consequences, or maladaptive behavior change; it does not require situational avoidance limited to the five agoraphobic domains. Persistent (>=2 weeks), meets full major depressive episode criteria, causes functional impairment. May include passive suicidal ideation or intrusive, distressing (ego-dystonic) thoughts of infant harm that the mother recognizes as wrong and resists. Subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis is the classic shoulder mimic of rotator cuff tendinopathy, producing overlapping lateral shoulder pain with overhead activity; the two frequently coexist (subacromial impingement can inflame both the cuff tendons and the overlying bursa), making pure clinical differentiation difficult without imaging in some cases. Similar tendon-bursa overlap occurs at other sites (e.g. retrocalcaneal bursitis mimicking insertional Achilles tendinopathy, olecranon bursitis near the elbow).

Tendinitis/tendinopathy adjacent to a bursa can mimic or coexist with bursitis (e.g., subacromial bursitis with rotator cuff tendinopathy, or trochanteric bursitis with gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy in GTPS); tenderness in tendinitis tends to localize along the tendon course and is reproduced by resisted contraction of that tendon's muscle, whereas bursitis tenderness is more focal over the bursa itself. In GTPS specifically, gluteal tendinopathy is frequently the primary pathology rather than the bursa.

Cellulitis produces diffuse, poorly-marginated skin erythema, warmth, and edema without a discrete fluctuant bursal collection; ultrasonography helps differentiate the two by showing (or not showing) a discrete distended bursal fluid collection, which is absent in isolated cellulitis. Cellulitis overlying a bursa can also coexist with, or progress to, septic bursitis.

Unlike fibromyalgia, rheumatoid arthritis presents with objective synovitis (joint swelling, warmth), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) and seropositivity (rheumatoid factor/anti-CCP) in most cases. Per the 2016 ACR fibromyalgia criteria, the two conditions can also coexist in the same patient, so a fibromyalgia diagnosis must not be used to explain away new objective inflammatory joint findings.

Polymyalgia rheumatica classically causes bilateral shoulder/hip girdle pain and stiffness in patients over 50, with markedly elevated ESR/CRP and a dramatic response to low-dose corticosteroids -- features absent in fibromyalgia, where inflammatory markers are normal.

Lumbar spondylosis (degenerative disc/facet disease) is the chronic background process on which many disc herniations occur; it is distinguished by more insidious-onset, activity-related axial low back pain without a dominant single nerve-root pattern, whereas acute disc herniation more often presents with sudden-onset radicular leg pain exceeding back pain and a positive straight-leg-raise sign referable to one nerve root. Elderly-onset/late-onset rheumatoid arthritis (LORA) can mimic PMR with proximal girdle symptoms. The 2012 EULAR/ACR criteria explicitly build in the distinction: points are awarded specifically for the ABSENCE of RF/ACPA (2 points) and the ABSENCE of peripheral joint involvement (1 point), i.e., presence of these features should push the diagnosis away from PMR and toward RA.
Not simply a differential but a genuinely overlapping/co-existing diagnosis with shared pathogenesis — see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE below for the real screening obligation this creates.

Cellulitis produces diffuse skin/soft-tissue erythema, warmth, and edema without deep bone involvement, whereas osteomyelitis involves the bone itself; MRI is the key discriminator because it can directly visualize marrow signal change (osteomyelitis) versus soft-tissue-only inflammation (cellulitis), with pooled MRI sensitivity 95.6% / specificity 80.7% for osteomyelitis.

Cross-referenced from this knowledge base's lumbar_spondylosis entry: pure lumbar spondylosis is facet/disc degeneration causing axial pain, radiculopathy, or neurogenic claudication WITHOUT measurable vertebral body translation. Spondylolisthesis is distinguished on the same lateral radiograph by a measurable anterior (or posterior) slip of one vertebral body on the next; degenerative spondylolisthesis and lumbar spondylosis otherwise share the same underlying facet/disc degenerative process and frequently coexist at the same level.

Cross-referenced from this knowledge base's herniated_intervertebral_disc entry: acute disc herniation typically presents more suddenly, with radicular leg pain exceeding back pain and a single dominant nerve-root pattern, and shows no vertebral slip on imaging - whereas spondylolisthesis-related radiculopathy develops on a background of a demonstrable pars defect or degenerative slip and is often more gradual in onset. The two can coexist, since disc degeneration is part of the same degenerative cascade that produces degenerative spondylolisthesis.

Cross-reference this knowledge base's dermatomyositis entry. Distinguished from PM by (1) presence of characteristic skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules) and (2) a complement/microangiopathy-mediated mechanism (capillary lysis, perifascicular atrophy) rather than PM's direct CD8+ T-cell/perforin attack on myofibers (Dalakas & Hohlfeld, PMID 14511932). In a real single-centre cohort, dermatomyositis had significantly lower CK than PM (316 vs 4884 U/L, p=0.005) despite comparable clinical weakness, consistent with the differing injury mechanisms.

Polymyositis (PM) is mechanistically and clinically distinguished from DM by the ABSENCE of the characteristic cutaneous findings (no heliotrope rash, no Gottron's papules/sign) - PM is a 'diagnosis of exclusion' among the IIMs requiring that skin disease and other identifiable causes (drug-induced myopathy, muscular dystrophy, IBM) be ruled out. Pathologically, PM shows endomysial CD8+ T-cell infiltration of non-necrotic, MHC-class-I-expressing fibers rather than the perifascicular, complement/microangiopathy pattern of DM.

Pityriasis rosea classically begins with a single larger 'herald patch' followed days to weeks later by smaller oval lesions distributed along skin cleavage lines (Langer's lines) in a 'Christmas-tree' pattern, each with a fine peripheral collarette of scale; it lacks the single, expanding, scaly-bordered ring of tinea corporis and is KOH-negative.

Rosacea is a key differential for facial acne-like eruptions in adults: it centres on the mid-face with persistent erythema, telangiectasia and inflammatory papules/pustules, but classically lacks comedones (a feature acne always has in some lesions), and it does not respond to standard acne therapy, requiring a distinct treatment strategy. Dermoscopically, features such as yellow/red halos, vascular polygons and follicular pustules have been shown to statistically differentiate rosacea from other facial inflammatory dermatoses.

MASLD is distinguished from alcohol-related liver disease (ALD) purely by quantified alcohol intake, since both can look histologically identical: MASLD requires intake <=20 g/day (female) / <=30 g/day (male); 'MetALD' is the overlap category (average 20-50 g/day female, 30-60 g/day male); intake above the MetALD range is classified as ALD (PMID 37363821). Global burden of liver disease: 2023 update. J Hepatol. 2023. PMID 36990226). Cross-reference this KB's "viral_hepatitis" entry.

Peptic ulcer disease shares H. pylori infection as its dominant cause and frequently coexists with the background chronic gastritis it arises from, but is defined endoscopically by a discrete mucosal break/crater at least 5 mm in diameter extending through the muscularis mucosae, which chronic gastritis alone does not have.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease produces heartburn/regurgitation that can overlap with epigastric dyspeptic symptoms, but is a distinct disorder of the gastro-oesophageal junction/lower oesophageal sphincter rather than a gastric mucosal inflammatory process.

Distinguishing features favoring diabetic nephropathy over primary CGN: long-standing diabetes (typically >5-10 years in type 1; variable in type 2), concurrent diabetic retinopathy, and a more gradual rise in proteinuria typically WITHOUT significant hematuria or RBC casts — active urinary sediment should prompt reconsideration of a primary/immune glomerular process and biopsy.

Nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) with edema/hypoalbuminemia/hyperlipidemia overlaps with (and in children is often used interchangeably to describe) several of the causal glomerular diseases underlying CGN, notably membranous nephropathy and FSGS. No dedicated 'nephrotic_syndrome' KB id was found in this database at the time of writing, so it is not cross-referenced by id for that reason.

confusable_name_raw: Bladder outlet obstruction / benign prostatic hyperplasia (in men) or pelvic organ prolapse (in women)
distinguishing_text: Mechanical outlet obstruction produces predominantly voiding symptoms (weak stream, hesitancy, straining, incomplete emptying) that can progress to overflow incontinence, mimicking detrusor underactivity; in women, advanced pelvic organ prolapse can itself kink the urethra and either mask or, after reduction, unmask stress incontinence. Pressure-flow urodynamics and a pelvic examination (looking for prolapse) are the distinguishing tools.

confusable_name_raw: Recurrent or chronic urinary tract infection (UTI)
distinguishing_text: IC/BPS diagnosis fundamentally requires excluding active bacterial infection: the AUA guideline's exclusion-based diagnostic framework and NIDDK's diagnostic description both make ruling out infection (via urinalysis and urine culture) a required first step, since UTI causes an overlapping symptom picture of urgency, frequency, and bladder/suprapubic pain but is treatable with antibiotics and should resolve, unlike IC/BPS. Persistent symptoms despite negative repeated cultures and appropriate antibiotic trials point away from ongoing infection and toward IC/BPS.
